structure.title: II. Context (Hindu-Muslim relations; the factory; dependency measure)
III. Research Design (randomization, timeline, balance, quasi-random task allocation)
V.A-B Results: production data and endline survey
VII. Discussion (supervisor survey and policy implications)

observations.statement: The paper states its estimand as the causal effect of randomly assigned religious team mixing on team output and attitudes, separately for high- and low-coordination production tasks, naming this a randomized field experiment.

The design deliberately avoids creating Muslim-only teams because they do not occur naturally, and the authors argue this choice limits demand effects and power problems while creating an identification limitation addressed later through indirect tests.

The randomization is described as a multi-step, constrained procedure carried out separately for each production line, moving workers between sections and cohorts to create two line-level team types while minimizing the number of workers who change task.

The main analysis draws on two data sources: firm administrative records of line-level output tied to revenue, and daily supervisor ratings of line-section-level team performance, supplemented by baseline and endline worker surveys.

The intervention window, baseline survey timing, and a COVID-19-constrained phone endline survey are stated explicitly and illustrated in a project timeline figure, with a separate later wave for supplementary belief and productivity data.
Attrition at endline is addressed with a footnote stating that attrition is balanced across treatment arms, pointing to a balance table that is only available in the online appendix.

The paper explicitly distinguishes three units of observation used across different tables: production line-level team-shift-day, line-section-level team-shift-day, and individual worker, and states which outcome data are available at each level.

Egg-room and flour-room teams are included in the individual-level and line-section-level samples but excluded from line-level team analysis because they serve all production lines and are not rated by supervisors, a distinction stated in a figure note.

Treatment is defined as a dummy for whether a line-section-level (or line-level) team is religiously mixed versus homogeneous, with the mixed share of Muslim workers targeted within a stated range during randomization.

The key task-level moderator, direct dependency, is constructed from stopwatch time-use measurements of minutes of continuous physical coordination per ten-minute period, then dichotomized into high- and low-dependency tasks using a median split, with alternative cutoffs checked in an appendix table.

Line-level output is measured in logs of pieces and of boxes produced; line-section-level output is a daily supervisor rating on a bounded scale, also recoded as an above-median indicator; individual attitude outcomes are coded from categorical survey response scales.
The line-level output regressions use log-transformed output as the dependent variable in both the pieces and boxes measures.

Several outcomes are built as standardized indices, including a combined index of the three endline attitude measures and a standardized index of baseline support for Hindutva politics used in heterogeneity analysis.

In the line-section and individual-level specifications, the treatment of interest is represented by two interaction terms, mixed status interacted separately with an HD indicator and an LD indicator, rather than by a single pooled mixed dummy.

The main results tables list which fixed effects are included as labeled rows, report observation counts and adjusted R-squared, and report the mean of the dependent variable directly beneath the coefficient block.

Table notes state explicitly at which level standard errors are clustered (line-level team for line-level output, line-section-level team for ratings, attitudes, and interactions) and describe how binary or categorical outcomes are coded.

A robustness table adds sets of interacted control variables sequentially across columns, letting the reader see how the two interaction coefficients of interest move as team-size, schooling, and tenure interactions are added one group at a time.

Several tables report a pooled specification and an interacted specification with HD/LD side by side in adjacent columns, along with a reported p-value for the equality of the two interaction coefficients.

Standard errors are clustered at the level at which treatment was assigned: the line-level team for line-level output regressions and the line-section-level team for section-, worker-teammate-, and individual-level regressions.

Because the line-level regressions have a stated small number of clusters, the paper additionally reports wild cluster bootstrap confidence intervals alongside the clustered standard errors, citing the Cameron-Gelbach-Miller bootstrap procedure.

Because the randomization procedure is nonstandard (constrained, multi-step, stratified reassignment), the paper justifies supplementing cluster-robust inference with randomization inference, re-running the randomization procedure many times and with permutation tests that reassign treatment across cohorts within a line or line section.

Balance checks for worker and team characteristics are reported at the line-section, line, and task levels, both with and without religion fixed effects, but the actual tables are located in the online appendix rather than the printed text.
Attrition analysis is reported only as a footnote claim (attrition balanced across arms) pointing to an online appendix table, without the underlying regression appearing in the main text.

A dedicated subsection argues that workers were quasi-randomly allocated to high- versus low-dependency tasks at baseline (via first-come-first-served hiring) and supports this with tenure-balance comparisons and a check that task-switching is uncorrelated with observables, with details deferred to an online appendix.

The paper reports two validation exercises for using supervisor ratings as a proxy for line-level output: a stated correlation between average section ratings and line output, and a check that mixed and nonmixed sections' ratings affect line output similarly, both housed in online-appendix figures.

A separate balance check compares HD and LD sections on non-work interaction, temperature, and noise to rule these out as confounding physical-environment differences, reported in an online appendix table.

Line-level output results are shown to be robust to alternative fixed-effect structures, including line-by-variety and line-by-day fixed effects, described in the main text with the detailed tables in the appendix.

Section-rating results are checked for robustness to including supervisor fixed effects, to controlling for schooling and tenure, and to alternative cutoffs for the high/low-dependency classification, all summarized in the main text with tables in the online appendix.

To rule out upstream-to-downstream spillovers in supervisor ratings, the paper restricts the sample to lines where HD sections follow LD sections and separately to only the first two sections of each line, and reports the main pattern still holds.

Robustness of the key interaction coefficients to every possible combination of the added control variables is summarized visually using a specification-curve-style coefficient plot generated with a named open-source R package.

Line-section-level and individual-level results are shown to be robust to clustering standard errors at the (coarser) line level instead of the line-section-level team, with the supporting tables placed in the online appendix.

Randomization-inference and permutation-test p-values are reported alongside cluster-robust p-values as an alternative inference procedure and described as yielding very similar conclusions about statistical significance.

Line-section-level dynamic treatment effects are split by whether Hindu workers' pre-intervention exposure to Muslim coworkers was above or below the median, motivated as a test of whether prior exposure explains away the main effect.

A separate heterogeneity analysis splits mixed teams by whether Hindu members' baseline support for Hindutva politics was above or below median, interpreted as evidence for a taste-based preference channel.

The paper explicitly flags that recoding the section-rating outcome as an above-median indicator was not part of the preregistration, distinguishing this specification from the preregistered primary analysis.

Survey-based worker-interaction outcomes (identifying a teammate as low-effort, being blamed by a teammate, willingness to sacrifice relief time) are used as intermediate evidence linking the treatment to the output effects rather than as endpoints in themselves.

The paper explicitly states it cannot make a conclusive judgment on the relative importance of the three candidate channels and repeatedly labels the supporting evidence as suggestive rather than definitive.
observations.quote: my data do not allow me to make a conclusive judgment

observations.statement: A separate short-term paper-bag manufacturing task with a new sample of Hindu and Muslim workers is run specifically to test, outside the main firm setting, whether Hindu-Muslim productivity differences (rather than coordination) could explain the results, with the mismatch in setting explicitly noted as a caveat.

An incentivized belief-elicitation module, in which participants predict coworker productivity by religion for a monetary reward, is used as evidence on in-group bias in beliefs as a candidate mechanism distinct from taste-based preferences.
The line-level output effect is translated into a monetary output-value difference using the average market price of the firm's products, in addition to being reported as a share of output.
The effect of HD-task mixing on the combined endline attitude index is reported in standard-deviation units of that index.

The paper situates its output-loss and attitude-change magnitudes against related quasi-experimental studies of ethnic or caste diversity in production teams, framing its contribution as extending this literature to a randomized, long-term team-assignment setting.

The absence of Muslim-only teams by design is explicitly acknowledged as a limitation that prevents directly testing whether Muslim workers are less productive on average, addressed instead through several indirect tests.

COVID-19 restrictions are stated to have forced the endline survey to be conducted by phone rather than in person, which the authors say prevented collecting a set of politically sensitive outcomes that respondents might be uncomfortable discussing over the phone.

The authors state that the experiment could not be extended for a longer follow-up period because the firm did not want to reform the teams again and because COVID-19-related restrictions intervened, limiting the observable duration of dynamic effects.

Evidence from the supplementary paper-bag task and the belief-elicitation exercise is explicitly caveated as coming from a different setting and sample than the main factory experiment, so those findings are called only suggestive for the main context.

The conclusion discusses how the balance of high- versus low-dependency work differs across agriculture, manufacturing, and services, framing this as an open question about how the paper's findings might generalize across stages of structural transformation.

Dynamic treatment effects are plotted over time-period bins for both line-level output and line-section-level ratings, with bootstrap wild-cluster confidence intervals shown as error bars at two confidence levels.
Tables use a conventional significance-star policy at three thresholds and table notes routinely state the unit of observation, the clustering level, and how each outcome variable is coded.

A descriptive table upfront lists the core production tasks, their productivity measures, and their dependency-score percentiles and HD/LD classification, serving as a reference table for the rest of the paper.
A specification-curve-style coefficient plot summarizing robustness across control-variable permutations is placed in the online appendix rather than the main text.

The introduction previews the paper's three key findings (output loss concentrated in high-dependency tasks, attenuation of that loss over time, and improved attitudes in high-dependency mixed teams) before the formal results sections.
The introduction closes with an explicit roadmap paragraph listing what each of the remaining numbered sections covers.

Several consecutive paragraphs in the introduction position the paper's contribution relative to distinct literatures (diversity and firm productivity, social preferences at work, intergroup contact), each with its own paragraph.

Robustness checks appear as a labeled subsection within the results section, followed by a separate later section on candidate channels/mechanisms and then a discussion section, and the main text repeatedly defers balance checks and most robustness tables and figures to an online appendix (appendices A-D) not part of the printed article.
observations.locator: Section I footnote 3; sections V.C, VI, VII headings

observations.statement: A Data Availability statement at the end of the article names a specific Harvard Dataverse repository with a DOI where code and data used to replicate the tables and figures are deposited.

The Data Availability statement specifies that only the nonproprietary portion of the data is shared, implying that some of the firm's administrative production data underlying the results is restricted and not deposited.

Data are described as coming both from proprietary firm administrative production records obtained through a partnership with the factory and from surveys the authors administered themselves at baseline and endline.

The front-matter footnote states that the study received ethics approval from two named institutional review boards and was preregistered in the American Economic Association registry, with the registry ID given.
A footnote explicitly flags one specific outcome recoding (binary above-median section rating) as not part of the preregistration, distinguishing it from the preregistered specifications.

concordance.paper_says: Line-level, line-section-level, and individual-level specifications are all OLS with a set of fixed effects (equations 1-3), estimated as standard linear regressions.
concordance.card_shows: Card records est=hdfe_ols for all four traced specs (s1-s4), using Stata's areg with an absorbed day fixed effect plus line/shift regressors.
concordance.note: The card's 'hdfe_ols' label (areg with absorb) matches the paper's stated OLS-with-fixed-effects specification.

concordance.paper_says: Equation (1) states line, shift, and day fixed effects for the line-level regression; equations (2)-(3) state line-by-section, shift, and day fixed effects.
concordance.card_shows: Card's fe field for s1/s2 lists only ['doy'] (the absorbed day fixed effect); the areg call additionally includes i.line and i.Shift as regressors, which the card does not list under 'fe'.
concordance.note: Line and shift are included as dummy regressors rather than absorbed terms, so the paper's three-way fixed-effect description is implemented but only the absorbed day effect is captured in the card's narrow 'fe' field.

concordance.paper_says: Standard errors for the line-level output regression are clustered at the line-level team (line-cohort) level.
concordance.card_shows: Card records se=cluster on 'line_team' for specs s1 and s2.

concordance.paper_says: Standard errors for the line-section-level rating regressions are clustered at the line-section-level team.
concordance.card_shows: Card records se=cluster on 'line_section_team' for specs s3 and s4.

concordance.paper_says: In addition to cluster-robust standard errors, the line-level output table reports wild cluster bootstrap confidence intervals because of the small number of line-level clusters.
concordance.card_shows: Card's package list records Stata's boottest command as called, consistent with wild-cluster-bootstrap inference, but does not attach this to a specific spec's se_type field.
concordance.note: Package evidence (boottest) corroborates the paper's stated use of wild cluster bootstrap for the line-level table.

concordance.paper_says: The paper explicitly notes that line-level regressions compare HD-Mixed lines to LD-Mixed lines, not mixed to fully homogeneous lines, because no homogeneous line-level team exists by design; homogeneous comparison groups only exist at the section/task level.
concordance.card_shows: The design record's treatment description is stated generically as 'religious composition of production team (mixed vs. homogeneous)', without distinguishing the line-level HD-Mixed-vs-LD-Mixed comparison from the section-level mixed-vs-nonmixed comparison.
concordance.note: This nuance about which comparison group applies at which level is stated in the paper's text but not reflected in the card's single generic treatment description.

concordance.paper_says: A dedicated robustness table adds team-size, schooling, and tenure interaction controls sequentially to test whether HD/LD or Hindu/Muslim differences beyond religion and coordination explain the results.
concordance.card_shows: The four specs traced in the card (s1-s4) do not include a control-augmented version of the line-section rating regression; no spec corresponds to the sequential-controls table.
concordance.note: The card's traced specs appear limited to the baseline forms; the extensive control-interaction robustness check described in the paper is not represented among them.

concordance.paper_says: The paper states that extensive balance checks were run at the line-section, line, and task levels and reports that randomization was successful, with results in appendix tables.
concordance.card_shows: Card's diagnostic record x1 (balance) is marked 'unknown'.
concordance.note: Balance checks are clearly present per the paper's text, but the recipe-card extraction could not confirm or locate this in the code files it read.

concordance.paper_says: A footnote states that attrition is balanced across treatment arms, referencing a supporting appendix table.
concordance.card_shows: Card's diagnostic record x2 (attrition) is marked 'not_found_in_scope'.
concordance.note: The paper makes an attrition-balance claim that the card's code-reading pass did not find within the files it examined.

concordance.paper_says: None of the described specifications (equations 1-3) mention any weighting scheme; all regressions appear to be estimated unweighted.
concordance.card_shows: Card records w=None for every traced spec (s1-s4).

concordance.paper_says: The printed main text alone contains six numbered tables (tables 1-6) and seven numbered figures (figs. 1-7), with many more tables and figures described as housed in the online appendix.
concordance.card_shows: Card records tables=3 and figures=2 for the traced portion of the replication code.
concordance.note: The card's output count reflects only the specs/outputs traced from the limited set of files read (files_read=7), not the full set of tables and figures reported in the printed paper.

concordance.paper_says: Data sources are stated as firm administrative production records (output tied to revenue) plus supervisor ratings and author-administered baseline/endline worker surveys.
concordance.card_shows: Card's design record describes the treatment as randomized religious composition of production teams, consistent with an RCT drawing on administrative/firm records for the output outcome.

gaps: No explicit discussion in the main text of a multiple-testing or family-wise error correction across the several worker-interaction outcomes (table 4) or the several attitude outcomes (table 5).
No formal ex ante power calculation or minimum-detectable-effect discussion is stated in the main text.
No explicit statement of informed-consent procedures for survey respondents beyond naming the two IRB approvals in the front-matter footnote.

Balance tables, most robustness tables, and most figures referenced throughout (appendices A-D, tables A.1-B.24, figs. B.1-C.16) are stated to be online-only and were not present in the 56-page source text, so their exact content could not be directly verified from this note.
No explicit statement of statistical software versions is given in the main text beyond naming specific Stata commands (areg, ritest) and one named R package (starbility).

reading.note: Read the full 56-page text sequentially: introduction, context, research design, econometric specification, results (production data, endline survey), robustness, channels/mechanisms, discussion, conclusion, and skimmed the data-availability statement and reference list. The paper's own appendices A-D (tables A.1-B.24, figs. B.1-C.16) are stated throughout to be available only online and are not part of this 56-page source text, so they were not read; all citations below are to the printed main text and its footnotes.
